newsitem.title: UK: Banks take punt on Eurotunnel debt accord.
newsitem.headline: Banks take punt on Eurotunnel debt accord.

text.p: Anticipation of Anglo-French channel tunnel operator Eurotunnel gaining approval from shareholders and lenders for its debt restructuring has prompted significant buying by banks wanting a piece of the deal.
"About two billion pounds has been traded to value investors in the last 12 months," one investment banker told Reuters.

Value investors are those who put their money into so-called distressed debt -- usually bonds or loans issued by companies which have hit difficulties and not been able to keep up their payments -- in anticipation of an improvement.
There is an active secondary debt market in Eurotunnel, created by original lenders who have since cut their losses and sold to value investors at a discount to the debt's original value.
"The average price (for the debt) is the low 40s and that looks attractive assuming everything goes through," said the banker, who declined to be named.
While the number of lenders to Eurotunnel has dropped to 174 from an original 225, bankers said those that remain could see the value of their holdings increase significantly.
Earlier Eurotunnel revealed that Lazard Freres had bought 700 million stg of its junior bank debt through the secondary market, topping the list of its main lenders with an 8.71 percent stake.
Lazards is not alone in buying the debt, which is now trading at around 45 percent of its face value, with Bankers Trust holding 4.27 percent and Merrill Lynch 3.82 percent.
This information was given as Eurotunnel executives unveiled details of its debt restructuring prospectus, which is being sent to bank lenders and shareholders.
Japanese banks were the biggest sellers of Eurotunnel debt, now numbering only 10 compared with an initial 37 and holding only eight percent of the total stock of junior debt compared to 19 percent.

A Eurotunnel executive said it was likely the U.S. banks -- which had upped their numbers to 26 from 15 percent and now hold 24 percent of the loans -- had bought a large part of the debt for their own account and some for investors.

Eurotunnel plans to issue a billion stg of equity notes, 1.2 billion stg of participating loan notes and 1.5 billon stg of resettable bonds. This leaves four billion stg of junior debt, or 45.1 percent, in loans.
But bankers played down the suggestion the banks had bought into Eurotunnel's debt in order to structure derivatives around the new instruments.
"People who play in distressed debt are not heavy users of derivatives," said one. "On the whole its a cash market rather than a derivative market."
"We're taking the risk that the restructuring goes through," he added.

While some shareholders, who have seen the price of their shares reduced to almost nothing, have protested about the terms of the restructuring package because it dilutes their holding, bankers said most are likely to give it the green light.
And the banks left in the lending group are not likely to stall further a plan which has taken years to thrash out and is seen as the only way of them reclaiming any of their original loans.
"They realise they have just got to give it the go-ahead," the first banker said.

For those who have bought into the deal, the value is in looking at the package as a whole and assessing what the various components will be worth once it is agreed and Eurotunnel recovers fully from the fire which has disrupted services.
Estimates of what the debt and the associated new instruments may be worth if the restructuring is approved range from the low 50s to the high 50s, with some suggesting even higher levels.
But the rewards are far from guaranteed. Not only is approval of the deal needed, but Eurotunnel's own forecasts and those of a bank's analysts need to be spot on.
"You've only made a good investment if your projections are right," said one banker.
